## WealthEdu: Parental Wealth and Tertiary Education

<!-- DRAFT: adapted from master_supporting_docs/paper_drafts/01_introduction_motivation.tex — edit me -->

Children of wealthy parents are far more likely to complete higher education
than children of poor parents. This gradient is one of the most robust
patterns in the study of intergenerational mobility, and higher education is
one of the main channels through which economic advantage passes from one
generation to the next.

The gradient admits two very different readings. Under a **resource**
interpretation, wealth has a causal effect: it relaxes constraints on
educational investment — covering living costs, insuring against the risk
that schooling doesn't pay off, or letting a family support a child through
years of forgone earnings. Under a **family-type** interpretation, wealth is
instead a marker for characteristics that produce both the parents' wealth
and the children's schooling — parental education, preferences, transmitted
ability, social networks. The same correlation is consistent with a real
policy lever or with a mere symptom of who wealthy families already are —
telling the two apart is the question this project takes up.

Finland's setting sharpens the test: tertiary education is tuition-free for
domestic students, so the most mechanical resource channel — the ability to
pay for school — is switched off. If parental wealth still shapes children's
educational attainment here, the operative channel must be something other
than tuition affordability. If the gradient instead disappears once family
type is held fixed, then wealth differences do little to *cause* educational
attainment, even where they're large.

This project uses Finnish administrative register data to decompose the
observed wealth–education gradient into a causal resource share and a
family-type component, and is under development, targeting outlets in labor
and education economics. <!-- TODO: confirm before naming specific target journals publicly -->
